newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-India doubles term contract buying of diesel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-India doubles term contract buying of diesel.

text.p: India has more than doubled annual term diesel imports to 3.74 million tonnes for 1997-1998 compared with a year earlier as exporters sought to secure market share in the face of a possible glut, industry sources said on Monday.

State-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) awarded a one-year term contract to import high speed diesel -- used mostly for transport -- for delivery from June 1997 to May 1998 at about 50 cents below last year's awarded price, traders said.
India's current term contracts call for the import of 1.3 million tonnes in the year to the end of May.
But the 1997/1998 tender agreement was likely to mean that India would cut monthly spot imports by about 20 percent, traders said.
"We have already seen this in the June spot import (tender)," one trader said.
Early this month, IOC bought 270,000 tonnes of 1.0-percent sulphur diesel for June delivery after it had secured 870,000 tonnes for May delivery.
Traders said they were not surprised by IOC's decision to buy more term cargoes as the offers were well below prevailing spot prices in the international market.
"They received some very low prices. I think they decided to take advantage of it," said a trader.

Traders said the low offers, particularly from Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC), reflected the problems some Middle East producers faced recently in selling their products due to soaring spot Singapore prices.

Middle East spot prices are tied to Singapore prices, so when the Singapore market rises, so does the Middle East market. This made it difficult for countries like Kuwait to compete against cheaper products from other regions, like the Mediterranean or North West Europe.
The surge in Singapore prices opened up a huge arbitrage window, leading to diesel shipments of up to three million tonnes to Singapore and Asia.
The imports displaced some traditional Middle East supplies to the East and cut some Gulf producers' market share in Africa in favour of Mediterranean suppliers, traders said.
But despite the higher volume awarded in the term tender, traders said they expected IOC would remain a major force in the spot markets in Asia.
"Indian diesel demand is growing by about 10 percent a year. I don't think their spot volume will be affected too much," one trader said.
India consumes about 30 million tonnes of diesel a year and just over one-third of this is imported, they said.
India's domestic refining capacity is not expected to rise sharply within the next two years. The first large expansions are not expected until 1999, analysts said.
But industry officials said India was expected to add additional annual refining capacity of 70 million tonnes during the ninth five-year plant, which began on April 1, 1997.
That is more than double current capacity of 61.55 million tonnes per year.
